{{nihongo|'''Awayamanoueno Shrine'''|阿波山上神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located on Mount Awayama in {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|qid=Q83273}}, {{ill|Higashiibaraki District, Ibaraki|ceb|Higashiibaraki-gun|es|Distrito de Higashiibaraki (Ibaraki)|fa|شهرستان هیگاشی‌ایباراکی، ایباراکی|fr|District de Higashiibaraki|id|Distrik Higashiibaraki, Ibaraki|it|Distretto di Higashiibaraki|ja|東茨城郡|ko|히가시이바라키군|lt|Higašiibarakio apskritis|pl|Powiat Higashi-Ibaraki|pt|Distrito de Higashiibaraki|th|อำเภอฮิงาชิอิบารากิ|uk|Повіт Хіґасі-Ібаракі|vi|Higashiibaraki, Ibaraki|zh|東茨城郡|qid=Q1154667}}, {{ill|Shirosato, Ibaraki|Q1203068|qid=Q1203068}}. It is also known by the alternative name “Furuki Myōjin.” It is identified with the “Awayamanoue Shrine” listed in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}. Its former shrine rank was {{ill|Q712534|lt=gōsha}}<ref name="nakamura30"/>. The annual festival is held on April 15<ref name="nakamura30"/>. {{nihongo|'''Awayamanoueno Shrine'''|阿波山上神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Hitachi Province]].

== Overview ==
Awayamanoue Shrine is located in the {{ill|Katsura, Ibaraki|ja|桂村 (茨城県)|ko|가쓰라촌 (이바라키현)|qid=Q6378175|lt=Katsura area}} in the northern part of Shirosato Town. {{ill|Japan National Route 123|af|Japan Nasionale Roete 123|ja|国道123号|ko|국도 제123호선 (일본)|zh_min_nan|Ji̍t-pún Kok-tō 123-hō|qid=Q6156750}} runs along the western edge of the shrine grounds. Despite the shrine name containing “mountain top” ({{ill|Sanjo|ja|山上|zh|山上|qid=Q11465835}}), the surrounding area is flat land sandwiched between the Naka River and the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Katsura River}}. According to the *{{ill|Jinja Kakuroku|Q11590708|qid=Q11590708}}*, there is a tradition recorded as follows: “According to the sayings of the elders, in ancient times Oyama Village was called Kami-Awayama (Upper Awayama), and Awa-no Village was called Shimo-Awayama (Lower Awayama). The shrine was located above the two villages; therefore, it came to be called Awayamanoue.” Based on this tradition, the shrine name originally did not include the meaning of “on the mountain.”

“Awa” (あわ) is an ancient place name found not only in the Engishiki entry for Awayamanoue Shrine but also in the Awa District of {{ill|Naka District, Ibaraki|Q1062968|qid=Q1062968}} recorded in the *{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Wamyō Ruijushō}}*. In the Naka District section of the *{{ill|Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|ja|常陸国風土記|zh|常陸國風土記|qid=Q11481687}}*, the passage “To the northeast of the district, an official station was established across the '''Awagawa''' (粟河)” appears; this “Awagawa” is another name for the Naka River and is said to derive from its passage through Awa District<ref name="fudoki"/>. Awa District is thought to have comprised the area of present-day “Awayama” together with the neighboring southern area of “Awa” (formerly {{ill|Katsura, Ibaraki|ja|桂村 (茨城県)|ko|가쓰라촌 (이바라키현)|qid=Q6378175|lt=Awa Village}}). The *Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi* states, “This is said to be the place where millet originated in Hitachi Province,” preserving a tradition that this area was the birthplace of millet cultivation in Hitachi.

The *Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi* also suggests that, because this area was well suited for millet cultivation, it was originally called “Awa” (written with the character for millet), but under the influence of the {{ill|Provinces of Japan|bar|Provinzn vo Japan|bcl|Mga probinsya kan Hapon|ca|Províncies del Japó|cs|Provincie v Japonsku|de|Provinzen Japans|eo|Historiaj provincoj de Japanio|es|Provincias de Japón|fa|ولایت‌های ژاپن|fi|Japanin provinssit|fr|Provinces du Japon|gl|Provincia histórica do Xapón|hak|Lin-chṳ-koet|he|פרובינציות יפן|id|Provinsi (Jepang)|it|Province dell'antico Giappone|ja|令制国|ko|율령국|lt|Japonijos žemės|nl|Provincies van Japan|pl|Prowincje Japonii|pt|Antigas províncias do Japão|ro|Provinciile Japoniei|ru|Провинции Японии|simple|Provinces of Japan|sk|Provincia (Japonsko)|sr|Провинције у Јапану|su|Propinsi Jepang|tl|Mga lalawigan ng Hapon|tr|Japonya'nın vilayetleri|uk|Провінції Японії|ur|جاپان کے صوبے|vi|Ryōseikoku|wuu|令制国|zh|令制國|zh_min_nan|Lēng-chè-kok|zh_yue|令制國|qid=Q860290|lt=Kōjirei (edict on auspicious characters)}}, the characters “阿波” were adopted instead<ref name="hitachi"/>. Medieval and later documents still contain place names using the character for millet, such as Awa District, Kami-Awa (Upper Awa), and Shimo-Awa (Lower Awa). In {{ill|Shōhei|de|Shōhei|fa|شوهی (دوره)|fr|Ère Shōhei|ja|正平 (日本)|ko|쇼헤이|ru|Сёхэй|simple|Shōhei|sr|Шохеи|sv|Shōhei|tr|Shōhei|zh|正平 (日本)|qid=Q1143587|lt=Shōhei}} 10 (1355), {{ill|Satake Yoshiatsu|ja|佐竹義篤|qid=Q11383463}} granted this area to Satake Yoshitaka, who took the name Ōyama and made Ōyama Castle on an island-like hill his residence<ref name="oyamaj"/>; “Ōyama” is said to be a phonetic corruption of “Awayama.” In addition, Yoshinari, a younger brother of {{ill|Satake Yoshimori|ja|佐竹義盛|qid=Q11383456}} who lived in this area, styled himself “Awa Gyōbu no Daibu” and was known as “Awa-dono.” The name “Ōyama” remained the old village name until the late {{ill|Edo period|ar|فترة إيدو|ast|Periodu Edo|az|Edo dövrü|bcl|Panahon nin Edo|be|Перыяд Эда|bg|Едо (период)|bn|এদো যুগ|bo|ཨེ་དོའི་དུས་སྐབས།|br|Marevezh Edo|ca|Període Edo|ckb|سەردەمی ئێدۆ|cs|Období Edo|cv|Эдо тапхăрĕ|da|Edo-perioden|de|Edo-Zeit|eo|Epoko de Edo|es|Período Edo|et|Edo ajastu|eu|Edo aroa|fa|دوره ادو|fi|Edo-kausi|fr|Époque d'Edo|gl|Período Edo|he|תקופת אדו|hi|एदो अवधी|hr|Edo (razdoblje)|hu|Edo-kor|id|Zaman Edo|is|Jedótímabilið|it|Periodo Edo|ja|江戸時代|jv|Jaman Édo|ko|에도 시대|lt|Edo laikotarpis|lv|Edo periods|mk|Едо (период)|mn|Эдогийн эрин|ms|Zaman Edo|nl|Edoperiode|nn|Edotida|oc|Periòde Edo|pl|Edo (okres)|pt|Período Edo|ro|Perioada Edo|ru|Период Эдо|simple|Edo period|sk|Obdobie Edo|sl|Obdobje Edo|sq|Periudha Edo|sr|Едо период|su|Période Edo|sv|Edoperioden|th|ยุคเอโดะ|tl|Panahong Edo|tok|tenpo pi kulupu lawa Eto|tr|Edo Dönemi|uk|Період Едо|ur|ایڈو دور|uz|Edo davri|vi|Thời kỳ Edo|war|Panahon Edo|wuu|江戶時代|zh|江户时代|zh_min_nan|Edo sî-tāi|zh_yue|江戶時代|qid=Q184963}} (the {{ill|Tenpō|Q1369045|qid=Q1369045}} era), when it was renamed {{ill|Sawayama|ja|沢山村|ko|사와야마촌|qid=Q11553149|lt=Awayama Village}}.

== Enshrined deity ==
; {{ill|Sukunabikona|Q3275687|qid=Q3275687|lt=Sukunabikona-no-Mikoto}}
* From a tradition in which a child-shaped deity descended upon a great cedar tree holding {{ill|Foxtail millet|Q161211|qid=Q161211|lt=ears of millet}} in his hand, the shrine is also known as “'''Furuki Myōjin'''” (also called “'''Sakariko Myōjin'''”<ref name="chimei"/><ref name="hitachi"/>). The *Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi* records that places such as Mount Furuki and Furuki Plain lay to the southwest of the main hall, indicating the existence of place names derived from this legend.
* The {{ill|Shintai|Q327532|qid=Q327532}} is a wooden standing statue in the form of a child. The *Shinpen Hitachi Kokushi* states, “The shintai is a wooden standing figure wearing {{ill|Sokutai|Q1156828|qid=Q1156828}},” while the *{{ill|Fuken Gōsha Meiji Jinja Shiryō|Q11486103|qid=Q11486103}}* records, “The sacred body is seated in the form of a child.”
* Sukunabikona-no-Mikoto is a deity associated with millet, as according to the *{{ill|Nihon Shoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935}}*, after completing the creation of the land, he was struck by a millet stalk (awagara) at {{ill|Awashima|Q11559761|qid=Q11559761}} and crossed over to the Eternal Land.
* The {{ill|Shinboku|Q48743901|qid=Q48743901}} is a {{ill|Cryptomeria|Q147388|qid=Q147388|lt=cedar}}. According to the shrine grounds’ “Origin of the Sacred Tree,” a gigantic cedar said to be over a thousand years old and revered as “Ōsugi-sama” once stood here as the second-generation sacred tree. However, it was struck by lightning on September 18, {{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}} 47 (1972), caught fire, and posed a danger of collapse, leading to its felling (approved by the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|Q908077|qid=Q908077}} on July 5, Shōwa 48). The current sacred tree was grown from a sapling of “Ōsugi-sama.”

== Subsidiary shrines ==
There are eight subsidiary shrines<ref name="meiji"/>: Hachiman Shrine ({{ill|Emperor Ōjin|ar|الإمبراطور أوجين|arz|الامبراطور اوجين|azb|اوجین (ایمپیراتور)|bn|সম্রাট ওজিন|cs|Ódžin|de|Ōjin|es|Ōjin Tennō|eu|Ōjin enperadorea|fa|امپراتور اوجین|fi|Ōjin|fr|Ōjin|hr|Ōjin|id|Kaisar Ōjin|it|Ōjin|ja|応神天皇|ka|ოძინი|ko|오진 천황|nl|Ojin|pl|Ōjin|pt|Ojin|ru|Император Одзин|sh|Car Ōjin|simple|Emperor Ōjin|sl|Cesar Odžin|sv|Ojin|th|จักรพรรดิโอจิง|tl|Emperador Ōjin|tr|Ōjin (imparator)|uk|Імператор Одзін|uz|Imperator Ōjin|vi|Thiên hoàng Ōjin|yo|Emperor Ōjin|zh|应神天皇|zh_min_nan|Ôzin Thian-hông|zh_yue|應神天皇|qid=Q317997}}), Fuji Shrine ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto}}), Hōsō Shrine ({{ill|Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|lt=Tsukuyomi|Q595520|qid=Q595520|qid=Q595520|lt=Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto}}), Tenman Shrine ({{ill|Sugawara no Michizane|ar|سوغاوارا نو ميتشيزانه|br|Sugawara no Michizane|ckb|سوگاوارا نۆ میچیزانێ|de|Sugawara no Michizane|es|Sugawara no Michizane|fa|سوگاوارا نو میچی‌زانه|fi|Sugawara no Michizane|fr|Sugawara no Michizane|id|Sugawara no Michizane|it|Sugawara no Michizane|ja|菅原道真|kk|Сугавара но Митидзане|ko|스가와라노 미치자네|la|Sugawara no Michizane|ms|Sugawara no Michizane|nl|Sugawara no Michizane|nn|Sugawara no Michizane|pl|Michizane Sugawara|pt|Sugawara no Michizane|ru|Сугавара-но Митидзанэ|sh|Sugawara no Michizane|sv|Sugawara no Michizane|th|สึกาวาระ โนะ มิจิซาเนะ|tr|Sugawara no Michizane|uk|Суґавара но Мітідзане|zh|菅原道真|zh_classical|菅原道真|zh_min_nan|Sugawara no Mitizane|qid=Q382005}}), Tennō Shrine ({{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Q272993|qid=Q272993|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto}}), Ise Shinmei Shrine, Inari Shrine ({{ill|Ukanomitama|lt=Ukanomitama|Q3080728|qid=Q3080728|qid=Q3080728|lt=Ukanomitama-no-Mikoto}}), and Tōshō Tenman Shrine. Some sources do not list the Ise Shinmei Shrine or the Tōshō Tenman Shrine.

== History ==
According to shrine tradition, it was founded in the first year of {{ill|Taihō (era)|Q1346269|qid=Q1346269|lt=Taihō}} ({{ill|701|Q23496|qid=Q23496}})<ref name="nakamura30"/>.

In volume 49 of the *{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981}}*, under the entry for the 9th day of the 12th month of Ninwa 2 (886), it is recorded: “Granted Jūgoi-no-ge to Jūgoi-no-jō to the '''Awa Deity''' of Hitachi Province,” indicating that the “'''Awa Deity'''” was promoted to Senior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade. In the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō*, it is listed as the minor shrine “'''Awayamanoue Shrine'''” among the seven shrines (two major and five minor) of {{ill|Hitachi Province|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353}} {{ill|Naka District, Tokushima|Q1156492|qid=Q1156492}}. In the former Katsura Village, there is also the minor shrine “Ishifune Shrine” of Naka District, Hitachi Province.

In Kennin 4 (1216), {{ill|Shinran|Q512934|qid=Q512934}} is said to have relied on Amida-ji Temple located here to establish the Ōyama hermitage and to make it a base for missionary activities in the Okunaka District of Hitachi (origin of the Ōyama hermitage). At the entrance to the approach road stands a stone monument marking the site of the Ōyama hermitage, along with an explanatory signboard, and an Enmei Jizō is enshrined there.

In Entoku 2 (1490), there is a tradition that {{ill|Satake Yoshikiyo|Q11383467|qid=Q11383467}}, lord of {{ill|Ōda Castle|Q5369726|qid=Q5369726|lt=Ōta Castle}}, prayed at this shrine for victory in battle when he was driven out of Magone Castle by treacherous retainers. Feeling the divine favor, Yoshikiyo is said to have followed the custom of the shrine’s parishioners of not displaying kadomatsu decorations at New Year (from *Jōhoku Kyōdo Tokuhon*).

From the medieval to early modern periods, the shrine was revered by successive local lords.
* In the 11th month of Tenbun 10 (1541), Ōyama Yoshizumi rebuilt the shrine buildings (as recorded on a ridge tag).
* In Tenshō 10 (1592), Ōyama Yoshikatsu carried out repairs (ridge tag).
* During the Edo period, {{ill|Tokugawa Nariaki|Q1323770|qid=Q1323770}}, lord of {{ill|Mito Castle|Q848997|qid=Q848997}}, donated 15 koku of shrine land and also repaired the shrine buildings<ref name="nakamura30"/>.

During the {{ill|Mito Rebellion|Q1040831|qid=Q1040831}}, fighting took place within the shrine grounds<ref name="nakamura30"/>.

Under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern shrine ranking system}}, the shrine was ranked as a gōsha.
